judge: Claude Code subagent, Claude Opus 5.5, fresh

items.label: A
items.critique: The arrest is staged with evidence ('the cut rope proves it') and a wry 'damp and snug little cellar', more set-up and wit than a Nox guard bark carries. The caps on RATHER look like an imitation of Westwood's emphasis.

items.label: B
items.critique: The '...' split and the '!?' are Nox-like. But 'unless you'd like to feel his boot' and 'I won't miss you!' read as a crafted gag running through all three lines, where Westwood's guards are usually blunter.

items.label: C
items.critique: A stock 'Halt! You are forbidden to pass!' and a flat line of directions, then a short send-off with 'boy'. Plain and functional, with the slightly stiff phrasing of the campaign.

items.label: D
items.critique: A list of petty city rules with a dry sting ('don't even think about wizardry'), then 'Oh, I forgot to mention, no loitering.' This is Westwood's deadpan civic humour exactly.

items.label: E
items.critique: A polite, slightly formal refusal ('The wilds hold far too many perils for the common man'), a curt 'Move on!', then a plain notice that the Mayor gave permission. This is the campaign's opening-town gatekeeping.

items.label: F
items.critique: An effusive greeting ('our beloved [Place]'), urgent exclamations and a comma-spliced warning about bandits. The earnest, slightly over-eager register is typical of Westwood's welcoming NPCs.

items.label: G
items.critique: The first line packs in too much: a gate shut by order, who to see, and the Ogres. Dialect is laid on ('Wanna', 'that don't make you'), and the 'later' line comments on the player's standing, a writerly touch.

items.label: H
items.critique: The mood-setting opener ('Hardly anybody comes up to this gate these days') gives the player nothing, and 'Back to town... Have a pleasant day!' clashes in tone. The final line is plain, but the set reads like a generic guard template.

items.label: I
items.critique: The guard explains his own job ('so nobody wanders up the north road and gets robbed blind'), which is exposition aimed at the player, and 'robbed blind' is idiom-flavoured. The 'Aiieee! Wolves!' panic is Nox-like but reads as borrowed.

items.label: J
items.critique: Bare and functional ('This is the home of [Person].'), with generic thanks and 'Adventurer'. It has the unadorned filler quality of many real Westwood guards.

tells: Westwood guards state one thing per line, flatly: a rule, a direction, a permission. The new texts pack two or three facts or a staged mini-scene (evidence, an arrest, gate orders plus a monster threat) into one bark.

The new texts lean on colloquial dialect and idiom ('Wanna', 'that don't make you', 'robbed blind', 'feel his boot') for flavour. Westwood's guards speak a plain, slightly formal standard English, and their humour comes from content (a list of petty rules), not slang.

Generated guards explain themselves or set a mood ('I guard this gate so...', 'Hardly anybody comes up here'). Westwood's guards open with a greeting, a command or a rule that tells the player what to do.
Westwood's tone is earnest or deadpan and consistent within a guard. The new texts swing between menace and cheer within one guard ('Back to town with you!' then 'Have a pleasant day!').
Imitated Nox markers (CAPS emphasis, '!?', 'Aiieee!') show up more densely in the generated texts than in Westwood's own.
